title: A Direct Instruction Horror Story
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman responds to season two of Emily Hanford's Sold a Story podcast on Direct Instruction by arguing that the scary stories told about the program are myths. He notes that evaluations found it helped children learn to read and do math and also raised problem-solving and self-esteem. His main critique is that the podcast tells the story of Direct Instruction the program rather than direct instruction the concept, meaning explicit teaching with clear explanations, modeling and guided practice. He draws on Kirschner, Hendrick and Heal's Instructional Illusions to argue that the discovery illusion confuses how experts create knowledge with how novices acquire it. He also cites the evidence that achievement predicts later motivation rather than the reverse, so success, not enthusiasm first, builds love of a subject. His conclusion is that explicit instruction is not the enemy of curiosity and that students need a base of knowledge before they can think critically.
points: Aldeman separates the Direct Instruction program from the broader idea of explicit instruction, which is the real question for how novices learn.
The claim that Direct Instruction is robotic or joyless is called a fairy tale, since evaluations found gains in reading, maths, problem solving and self-esteem.
Kirschner, Hendrick and Heal's discovery illusion is the category error of treating how experts discover as how novices should learn.
The cited longitudinal evidence says achievement predicts later motivation, not the other way round, so early success helps build interest.
Students need a solid knowledge base before they can analyze or write critically, which explicit instruction can supply.
quotes: In fact, those are fairy tales that adults made up about a program called Direct Instruction. In the real world, when researchers went to evaluate it, they found that it helped kids learn to read and do math, and it also helped them to build up their problem-solving skills and self-esteem.
My biggest critique —and there are only four episodes so far!—is that Hanford has told the story of Direct Instruction the program as opposed to direct instruction the concept.
Perhaps most fundamentally, the discovery illusion rests on a profound category error: the confusion between how experts create knowledge and how novices acquire it.

Expecting students to learn primarily through discovery is akin to expecting someone to compose symphonies before mastering musical notation; it fundamentally misunderstands the prerequisites for meaningful discovery.
Students who experienced success in mathematics developed greater intrinsic motivation towards maths over time, but higher motivation alone did not lead to improved achievement.
The broader lesson here is that we should be wary of spooky stories about explicit or direct instruction. It is not the enemy of curiosity or motivation. Far from it.
They need a solid base of knowledge to exercise those skills, and some amount of carefully constructed direct instruction can often help them get there.
